blocks.text: **The problem.** You are given an array of intervals, where `intervals[i] = [start, end]`. Merge all **overlapping** intervals and return the non-overlapping intervals that cover exactly the same ranges.

blocks.alt: Four intervals on a number line: [1,3], [2,6], [8,10] and [15,18]. The first two overlap and merge into [1,6]; the others stay as they are.

blocks.code:
Input:  [[1,3], [2,6], [8,10], [15,18]]
Output: [[1,6], [8,10], [15,18]]      [1,3] and [2,6] overlap, so they become [1,6]

Input:  [[1,4], [4,5]]
Output: [[1,5]]                       touching intervals count as overlapping

blocks.text: Two intervals overlap when one starts **before (or exactly when) the other ends**. Merging them gives an interval from the earlier start to the **later** end. Think of meetings in a calendar: back-to-back or overlapping meetings merge into one busy block.
The input isn't sorted — the classic test case lists `[15, 18]` before `[2, 6]` — and that's what makes it feel hard at first.
1. Brute force: merge overlapping pairs until none are left
Look for any two intervals that overlap, replace them with their merge, and start looking again. When a full search finds no overlapping pair, every interval is separate.
**Time O(n³), space O(n).** Each merge removes one interval, there can be n − 1 merges, and finding each one can take O(n²) comparisons.
2. Optimal: sort by start, then one pass

Sort the intervals by their start. Now any interval that could overlap the one you're building must come **right after it**: once an interval starts after the current end, every later interval starts even later, so none of them can reach back.

So after sorting, one pass is enough. Keep the last merged interval; for each next interval, either it **overlaps** (extend the end) or there's a **gap** (the last interval is final — start a new one).

blocks.alt: Snapshots of the merge pass over the sorted intervals [1,3], [2,6], [8,10], [15,18]. [2,6] overlaps [1,3] and stretches it to [1,6]. [8,10] starts after 6, so a new interval begins. [15,18] starts after 10, so another begins.

blocks.text: **Why `max` is essential.** The obvious-looking `last.end = current.end` is wrong, and it fails on **nested** intervals. Take `[[1, 10], [2, 3]]`: they overlap, but `[2, 3]` sits entirely **inside** `[1, 10]`, so the merged end must stay 10 — not shrink to 3.
**Time O(n log n), space O(n).** The sort dominates; the pass itself is O(n). The `merged` list is a second copy of the data — but notice it never holds more intervals than we've already read.
3. Best solution: merge in place with a write pointer

Since the merged intervals never outnumber the ones already read, they can be written **back into the input array**. `read` walks forward; `write` points at the interval currently being built. Overlap? Stretch `intervals[write]`. Gap? Move `write` forward and copy the new interval there. At the end, cut the array after `write`. It's the same reader/writer idea as **Move Zeroes**.

blocks.alt: After the in-place pass over [1,3], [2,6], [8,10], [15,18], the first three slots hold [1,6], [8,10] and [15,18], with write pointing at slot 2. The last slot is a leftover copy and gets cut off.
blocks.caption: No second list: the answer grows at the front of the array it was read from.
Enter [start,end] pairs in any order — the first step sorts them. Try the Nested example to watch max keep the end at 10.

blocks.text: **Time O(n log n), space O(1)** extra beyond the sort — the answer lives in the input array. In Java, `Integer.compare(a[0], b[0])` is safer than `a[0] - b[0]`, which can overflow; in C++, sorting vectors compares them element by element, which sorts by start first.

rows.approach: Brute force: merge overlapping pairs until none are left
rows.timeWhy: Up to **n − 1** merges, and finding each overlapping pair can take **O(n²)** comparisons.
rows.spaceWhy: A working copy of the intervals.

rows.approach: Optimal: sort by start, then one pass
rows.timeWhy: The **sort dominates**; the merging pass after it is O(n).
rows.spaceWhy: The `merged` list is a **second copy** of the data.

rows.approach: Best: merge in place with a write pointer
rows.timeWhy: Still the **sort**, then one O(n) pass.
rows.spaceWhy: Merged intervals are written back **into the input**; only a write index is extra.

blocks.text: Nothing can beat O(n log n) here in general, because the input arrives unsorted. The best solution's win is memory: it reuses the array it was given instead of building a second list.
"Sort by start, then sweep once" also inserts a new interval into a sorted list, counts how many meeting rooms are needed, and finds the busiest moment of a schedule.
